headline: UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, ONS says

terms.meaning: The total value of goods and services an economy produces in a period.
A three-month period; Quarter 3 is July to September.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences borrowing costs.

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, ONS says
levels.body:
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) estimates that UK real GDP rose by 0.7% in Quarter 3 (July to September) 2026, following growth of 0.5% in Quarter 2. Output was 1.9% higher than in the same quarter a year earlier.
Services grew by 0.9% and production by 0.1%, while construction shrank by 0.7%. The ONS said information and communication has been the largest driver of growth across 2026, with many fast-growing firms linked to artificial intelligence and cloud computing. Quarter 1 growth stands at 0.6%, and Quarter 2 was revised up from 0.4%.
The figures matter for the Bank of England, which raised Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November. Analysts quoted by CNBC said the data keep a December rate rise firmly on the table, and LSEG data put the market chance of a rise at 73%. The Bank has projected that growth will slow in the final quarter of the year and into 2027.
levels.why: Strong growth gives the Bank of England room to keep raising rates to fight inflation, which affects mortgages, savings and jobs.

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.7% from July to September
levels.body:
The ONS says UK real GDP grew by 0.7% in the third quarter of 2026, after 0.5% growth in the second quarter. That leaves the economy 1.9% bigger than a year earlier.
The growth was led by services, which rose 0.9%. Production edged up 0.1%, but construction fell 0.7%. The ONS singled out information and communication, where fast-growing firms linked to AI and cloud computing have driven much of this year's expansion. Growth in the first quarter was 0.6%, and the second quarter was revised up from an earlier 0.4%.
The numbers keep a December interest rate rise firmly in view, according to analysts. The Bank of England lifted Bank Rate to 4% earlier this month, and markets see a 73% chance of another rise. The Bank itself expects growth to slow towards the end of the year and into 2027.
levels.why: The figures help decide whether interest rates rise again next month, which affects anyone with a loan or mortgage.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.7% as AI-linked firms and services lead the way
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September, the Office for National Statistics has said, up from 0.5% in the previous three months. Compared with a year ago, output is 1.9% higher.
Services did most of the work, growing 0.9%. Production rose slightly by 0.1%, while construction contracted by 0.7%. The ONS said technology and communications firms, many linked to artificial intelligence and cloud computing, have been the biggest source of growth in 2026.
The strong figure matters because the Bank of England raised its main interest rate to 4% on 5 November to fight rising prices. Analysts say another rise in December is firmly possible, and traders put the odds at 73%. The Bank expects growth to slow in the final months of the year and during 2027.
levels.why: Healthy growth makes another interest rate rise more likely, which would affect borrowers and savers.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.7% in three months to September
levels.body:
Britain's economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter of the year, the Office for National Statistics said on Thursday. That compares with 0.5% growth in the second quarter and puts the economy 1.9% above its level a year earlier.
Shops, banks, technology firms and other services grew by 0.9%. Factories and other production rose by 0.1%, but construction shrank by 0.7%. The ONS said technology and communication businesses, many working on artificial intelligence and cloud computing, have driven growth this year.
The news comes after the Bank of England raised interest rates to 4% to curb inflation. Analysts think another rise in December is likely, and the Bank has warned that growth will probably slow before the end of the year.
levels.why: The growth figures will influence whether the Bank of England raises interest rates again, which affects household budgets.

levels.headline: UK economy grew faster than before between July and September
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September, official figures show. That is faster than the 0.5% growth in the previous three months. Over the past year the economy has grown by 1.9%.
Most of the growth came from services, such as shops, banks and technology firms, which grew by 0.9%. Factories and other producers grew only slightly, and the building industry shrank by 0.7%. The Office for National Statistics said many fast-growing firms work with artificial intelligence (AI) and cloud computing.
The Bank of England recently raised its main interest rate to 4% to slow price rises. Experts think it could raise the rate again in December. The Bank also expects the economy to grow more slowly at the end of this year and next year.
levels.why: Strong growth can mean more jobs, but it may also lead to higher interest rates on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew by 0.7% in three months
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% between July and September. Economists measure this using GDP, which is the total value of everything a country makes and sells. A year ago the economy was smaller, so over twelve months it has grown by 1.9%.
Most of the growth came from services, which means jobs like shop work, banking and computer work. These grew by 0.9%. Building work fell by 0.7%. Some of the fastest-growing firms use artificial intelligence, or AI, and cloud computing.
The Bank of England has just put up its main interest rate to 4%. This is meant to stop prices rising too quickly. Many experts now think it will raise the rate again in December. The Bank says growth is likely to slow down soon.
levels.why: Growth is good for jobs, but it can lead the Bank to raise interest rates, which makes borrowing dearer.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew over the summer
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% from July to September. The economy is everything people make, sell and buy in the country. When it grows, there is usually more work and more money moving around. Over a whole year it has grown by 1.9%.
Shops, banks and computer firms did well. Building work got smaller. Many fast-growing firms use AI, which is clever computer software.
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. It has put up its interest rate to 4%. An interest rate is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or earn when you save. The Bank did this to stop prices rising too fast. It may do it again in December. It also thinks growth will slow soon.
levels.why: It shows how the economy is doing, and it may change how much people pay on loans.

levels.headline: The country's money machine grew a bit more
levels.body:
Britain's economy grew by 0.7% between July and September. The economy is all the things people make and sell, like food, phones and haircuts. When it grows, it gets bigger. Over one year it has grown by nearly 2%.
The biggest growth came from jobs like shops, banks and computer work. Building got smaller. Some firms use AI, which means computers that can learn and help with tasks.
The Bank of England keeps an eye on prices. It has made borrowing cost more, to stop prices going up too fast. A cost for borrowing is called interest. The Bank might make it cost more again in December. It thinks the economy will grow slower soon.
levels.why: It tells us if the country is doing well, and whether borrowing might cost more.

levels.headline: The country got a bit richer over the summer
levels.body:
Between July and September, the country made and sold more things than before. Think of the country like one big shop and factory. In those three months it did 0.7% more business than the three months before. That is a small step up.
Shops, banks and computer firms did well. People who build houses and roads did less work. Some firms are using AI, which are smart computer programs.
There is a group called the Bank of England. It looks after the country's money. It has made borrowing more costly, so prices stop climbing too fast. If you borrow money, you pay a bit extra back. This is called interest. The Bank might raise it again soon.
levels.why: It shows whether the country is doing well and whether borrowing might cost more.

levels.headline: Imagine the whole country is one big school fair
levels.body:
Imagine the whole country is one big school fair. Everyone makes things and sells them, like cakes, crafts and games. Between July and September, the fair got a little busier than before. There were 0.7% more things made and sold.
The stalls selling things and helping people did best. The stall building new things did a bit worse. Some stalls now use clever computers called AI to help them.
The fair has a grown-up called the Bank of England, who looks after the pocket money. When things get too pricey, the grown-up asks people to pay a little extra when they borrow. That extra is called interest. The grown-up has done this lately, and might do it once more.
levels.why: It tells us the country is busy and doing well, and borrowing may cost a little more.

headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.35% as Nvidia falls after chief executive resigns

terms.meaning: An index tracking the share prices of 500 large US companies.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, an index of 30 big US companies.
A chief executive who leads a company temporarily until a permanent one is chosen.

levels.headline: S&P 500 closes down 0.35% as Nvidia falls after chief executive resigns
levels.body:
The S&P 500 closed lower on Thursday 12 November, the latest completed session, falling 0.35% to 7,592.40. The Nasdaq Composite lost 0.39% to 25,366.09, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 189.40 points, or 0.36%, to 52,297.09.
Nvidia was the main drag. Its shares closed down 4.34% after chief executive Jensen Huang announced he was resigning as CEO and from the board. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim chief executive while the board searches for a permanent successor. Nvidia had been down by as much as 14% earlier in the day, and it makes up about 6% of the S&P 500.
The broader market recovered from early losses as investors moved past the announcement. Oil prices rose on the day, which also lifted Treasury yields. Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on 17 November under interim leadership.
levels.why: Nvidia is one of the biggest companies in the world, so its share price moves pensions and funds that hold the wider market.

levels.headline: US shares end lower as Nvidia drops on its chief executive's exit
levels.body:
The S&P 500 finished Thursday 12 November down 0.35% at 7,592.40. The Nasdaq Composite fell 0.39% to 25,366.09, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 189.40 points, or 0.36%, to close at 52,297.09. That was the last completed trading session.
Nvidia dragged the market after Jensen Huang announced he was stepping down as chief executive and as a board member. Its shares closed 4.34% lower, having fallen by as much as 14% during the day. Finance chief Colette Kress is interim chief executive. Nvidia makes up roughly 6% of the S&P 500, so its fall weighed on the index.
The wider market recovered much of its early losses. Oil prices rose, pushing up Treasury yields. Nvidia reports quarterly results on 17 November.
levels.why: Because Nvidia is so large, one company's news can move the whole US market and the funds that track it.

levels.headline: Wall Street slips as Nvidia tumbles after Huang resigns
levels.body:
US stocks closed lower on Thursday 12 November. The S&P 500 fell 0.35% to 7,592.40, the Nasdaq dropped 0.39% to 25,366.09, and the Dow lost 189.40 points, or 0.36%, to 52,297.09.
The chipmaker Nvidia led the fall. Its shares ended down 4.34% after chief executive Jensen Huang said he was resigning. The company's finance chief, Colette Kress, will run it for now while a permanent boss is found. Nvidia shares had been down as much as 14% earlier, and the firm makes up about 6% of the S&P 500.
The market steadied during the day as investors looked past the news. Oil prices rose, which pushed up the interest rates on US government debt. Nvidia publishes results on 17 November.
levels.why: Nvidia is a key company in the AI boom, so worries about it can shake investors well beyond one share price.

levels.headline: US shares fall as Nvidia boss quits
levels.body:
Shares in the United States ended lower on Thursday. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 large companies, fell 0.35% to 7,592.40. The Nasdaq, which has many technology firms, lost 0.39% and closed at 25,366.09. The Dow, which covers 30 large companies, dropped 189.40 points, or 0.36%, to 52,297.09.
The biggest faller was Nvidia, the chip company at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom. Its shares ended 4.34% lower after chief executive Jensen Huang announced his resignation. Finance chief Colette Kress will lead on a temporary basis. Nvidia is so large that it makes up about 6% of the S&P 500.
The market recovered some early losses. Nvidia's next results are due on 17 November.
levels.why: A big company's leadership change can move share prices, and many pension and savings funds hold these shares.

levels.headline: US shares end the day lower after Nvidia boss resigns
levels.body:
US shares ended Thursday a little lower. The S&P 500, an index of 500 big American companies, fell 0.35% to 7,592.40. The Nasdaq, full of technology firms, dropped 0.39% to 25,366.09. The Dow, which follows 30 large firms, lost 0.36% and finished at 52,297.09.
Nvidia, a company that makes computer chips used for artificial intelligence, was the main reason. Its boss, Jensen Huang, said he was resigning, and the share price fell 4.34%. Its finance chief, Colette Kress, will run the company for now. Nvidia is so big that it makes up about 6% of the S&P 500.
Earlier in the day the fall was much bigger, but the market recovered a lot. Nvidia reports its latest results on 17 November.
levels.why: Nvidia is so big that news about it can pull down the whole market, including savings and pension funds.

levels.headline: US shares fall a little as Nvidia's boss leaves
levels.body:
US shares fell a little on Thursday. A stock market is where people buy and sell small parts of companies, called shares. The S&P 500, a list of 500 big American companies, went down 0.35%. The Nasdaq went down 0.39%, and the Dow went down 0.36%.
The main reason was Nvidia. It makes the computer chips that help power AI. Its boss, Jensen Huang, said he was leaving. People got worried, and the price of its shares dropped by 4.34%. A manager called Colette Kress will do the job for now, until a new boss is found.
Nvidia is very big, so when it drops, the whole list drops too. Later in the day, things settled down.
levels.why: Share prices affect the money in many pensions and savings, so big moves are watched closely.

levels.headline: US shares dip as a big computer company loses its boss
levels.body:
On Thursday, share prices in America went down a little. Shares are tiny pieces of a company that people can buy. The S&P 500 is a list of 500 big companies, and its price fell by about one third of one percent. The Nasdaq and the Dow, two other lists, fell by about the same.
The big reason was Nvidia, a company that makes chips for clever computers. Its boss, Jensen Huang, said he was leaving. A woman called Colette Kress, who looks after the company's money, will lead for now.
Nvidia is so huge that when its shares fall, the whole list falls too. Many people watch share prices because pensions and savings are linked to them.
levels.why: Many people's savings are tied to share prices, so these small changes get watched closely.

levels.headline: US shares dip because a big company's boss left
levels.body:
On Thursday, share prices in America went down a tiny bit. Shares are small slices of a company that people can own. When lots of people want to sell, the price goes down. The prices of three big lists of companies all fell by about a third of one percent.
The biggest reason was a company called Nvidia. It makes the brains for clever computers. Its boss said he was leaving the job. People were worried, so they sold, and the price of its shares dropped.
A woman called Colette Kress will be the boss for now. Nvidia is so big that when it falls, the lists fall too. Later in the day, things calmed down.
levels.why: Lots of families have savings linked to share prices, so people keep an eye on them.

levels.headline: The big toy shop lost its boss, so prices wobbled
levels.body:
Imagine a giant toy shop that everyone knows. Its boss said, 'I am leaving.' People worried and some sold their little pieces of the shop. A piece of a company is called a share. When many people sell, the price goes down.
This happened on Thursday in America. The company is called Nvidia, and it makes the brains inside clever computers. Its share price fell. Because it is a very big shop, the whole market wobbled a tiny bit.
A kind helper called Colette will be the boss for now, until a new one is chosen. By the end of the day, things were calmer.
levels.why: Big companies matter to many people's savings, so wobbles get noticed.

levels.headline: When the head teacher leaves, everyone wonders what happens next
levels.body:
Imagine your school's head teacher said, 'I am leaving today.' Everyone would wonder what happens next. Some grown-ups might get a bit worried. That is a little like what happened to a very big company called Nvidia.
Its boss left his job, and people who own tiny pieces of the company, called shares, got worried. Some sold them, and the price went down. Because Nvidia is so big, other prices went down a little too, like a wobble in a line of toppling blocks.
A helper called Colette will lead the company for now, like a stand-in teacher. By the end of the day things were calmer.
levels.why: Many families have savings linked to company shares, so big changes are watched closely.

headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% and warns inflation will near 5%

terms.meaning: The Bank of England's main interest rate.
The group of nine experts who vote on interest rates.
The rate at which prices rise over time.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises Bank Rate to 4% and warns inflation will near 5%
levels.body:
The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1 on 5 November to raise Bank Rate by a quarter of a point, from 3.75% to 4%. It was the first increase since August 2023. One member wanted a bigger half-point rise to 4.25%.
The Bank said it now expects inflation to reach about 5% by the middle of 2027, up from 3.5% in September. It tied the outlook to energy prices and the conflict in the Middle East, including disruption around the Strait of Hormuz. Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise should not be seen as the first of an inevitable long run of increases, but added that unless the conflict is resolved it does not seem likely to be the last.
Markets put the chance of a further rise at the next meeting, on 17 December, at 73%. HMRC interest rates, which follow Bank Rate, will also go up.
levels.why: Higher Bank Rate raises costs for people with variable mortgages and loans, and it can lift returns for savers.

levels.headline: Bank of England lifts rates to 4%, first rise in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England raised Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4% on 5 November, its first rise since August 2023. The Monetary Policy Committee voted 8-1, and the one dissenter wanted a rise of half a point.
The Bank forecasts that inflation will reach about 5% by mid-2027, compared with 3.5% in September. It blames higher energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East and shipping disruption near the Strait of Hormuz. Governor Andrew Bailey said the rise was not the start of a certain long series, but that it does not look like the last unless the conflict is resolved.
Traders see a 73% chance of another rise at the next meeting on 17 December. Tax interest rates charged by HMRC will also increase.
levels.why: The decision changes borrowing costs for households and firms, and shows how global events reach UK finances.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4% as inflation set to climb
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%, the first increase in more than three years. Eight of the nine members of the rate-setting committee voted for the quarter-point rise, and one wanted a half-point rise.
The Bank warned that inflation, currently 3.5%, will climb to roughly 5% by the middle of 2027. It said higher energy prices linked to the Middle East conflict are the main cause. Governor Andrew Bailey said this should not be seen as the first of many rises, but it is unlikely to be the last unless the conflict ends.
Markets think there is a 73% chance of another rise on 17 December. The interest rates HMRC charges on late tax payments will rise too.
levels.why: Borrowers could face higher bills, while savers may earn more, so it touches most households.

levels.headline: Bank of England raises interest rates for the first time in over three years
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4%, the first rise since August 2023. Eight members of its committee backed the quarter-point increase, and one wanted a larger rise.
The Bank said it expects inflation, which measures how fast prices rise, to reach about 5% by the middle of next year. In September it was 3.5%. The Bank blamed higher energy costs linked to the war in the Middle East. Governor Andrew Bailey said the move was not the start of a long run of rises, but that more could follow if the conflict continues.
Markets think there is a good chance of another rise in December. HMRC's interest rates on late tax bills will go up as well.
levels.why: People with mortgages or loans may pay more, while savers may get better rates.

levels.headline: Interest rates go up to 4% as the Bank of England fights rising prices
levels.body:
The Bank of England has raised its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%. This is the first rise for more than three years. Eight of the nine experts who decide the rate voted for a small rise, and one wanted a bigger one.
The Bank says prices will probably rise faster in the coming months. It expects inflation, the speed at which prices go up, to reach about 5% by the middle of next year. It says higher energy prices from the war in the Middle East are the main reason. The Bank's governor, Andrew Bailey, said this might not be the last rise.
It will decide again on 17 December. Many people expect another rise then.
levels.why: It can make loans and mortgages cost more, but it can also help savers earn more.

levels.headline: The Bank of England puts up interest rates to 4%
levels.body:
The Bank of England has put up its main interest rate from 3.75% to 4%. An interest rate is the extra money you pay when you borrow, or earn when you save. This is the first rise in over three years.
The Bank did this because prices are going up faster. Inflation means prices rise over time, so a pound buys less. The Bank thinks it could reach 5% by the middle of next year. Higher energy prices from the war in the Middle East are the main reason.
The Bank's boss, Andrew Bailey, said more rises could come if the war goes on. The next decision is on 17 December.
levels.why: Loans and mortgages may cost more, but savings may earn more.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost more
levels.body:
The Bank of England has made borrowing money cost more. Its interest rate has gone up from 3.75% to 4%. This is the extra amount people pay when they borrow money. It is also the extra a bank pays you for saving.
The Bank did this because prices are going up fast. When prices go up, your pocket money buys less. Making borrowing cost more can slow that down. The Bank thinks prices might rise by about 5% over a year by next summer. Fuel and gas are costing more because of a war far away.
The Bank's boss said more rises might come. The next choice is on 17 December.
levels.why: It can change how much families pay on loans and how much they earn from savings.

levels.headline: The Bank of England makes borrowing cost a bit more
levels.body:
There is a bank for the whole country. It is called the Bank of England. It has made borrowing cost a bit more. The extra cost is called interest. It went up from 3.75 to 4 out of every 100 pounds.
The bank did this because prices are rising fast, and it may get faster. Gas and fuel cost more because of a war far away. If prices rise too fast, your pocket money buys less.
When borrowing costs more, people spend less. That helps slow prices down. The bank's boss said it might happen again. The next choice is on 17 December.
levels.why: It can change what families pay for loans and what they earn from saving.

levels.headline: The big bank put up its price for borrowing
levels.body:
Imagine you lend a friend a toy, and ask for a small treat back as thanks. That small treat is a bit like interest. The Bank of England is the biggest bank in the country, and it has raised the treat it asks for when money is lent.
It did this because the price of things is going up fast. Fuel and gas cost more because of a war far away. If prices go up too much, pocket money buys less sweets.
When borrowing costs more, people spend a little less, and that slows price rises down. The bank might do it again next month.
levels.why: It changes what families pay when they borrow and what they get when they save.

levels.headline: Why the sweet shop prices are creeping up
levels.body:
Imagine the sweet shop raising prices every week. Your pocket money would buy fewer sweets each time. That is called inflation, and the grown-ups at the Bank of England want to stop it growing.
They have a trick. They make it cost a bit more to borrow money. The extra cost is called interest. It went up a little this week, from 3.75 to 4. When borrowing costs more, people spend less, and shops stop raising prices so fast.
Prices are going up partly because of a war far away that makes fuel dearer. The grown-ups said they might use the trick again next month.
levels.why: It tries to keep prices steady so that pocket money, wages and savings keep their value.

headline: UK becomes first country to sanction all ten of Russia's major oil producers

terms.meaning: Penalties, such as financial restrictions, placed on a country or company.
Ageing tankers used to carry sanctioned oil in ways that avoid restrictions.
A forum of leaders from around 50 European countries, including non-EU members such as the UK.

levels.headline: UK becomes first country to sanction all ten of Russia's major oil producers
levels.body:
The UK government says it has sanctioned all ten of Russia's major oil producers, making it the first country to do so. The package also covers shadow fleet vessels involved in transporting Russian oil and liquefied natural gas, major coal companies, and Rosneft's flagship Arctic project, LLC Vostok Oil.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who took office on 20 July 2026, announced the move as he attended the ninth European Political Community summit in Dublin, hosted by Ireland. He planned to urge leaders from around 50 countries to keep piling pressure on Vladimir Putin and to push for robust, legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine. He is also due to co-chair a Friends of Ukraine event with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin.
The government said peace talks have progressed but that now is not the time for complacency, and urged pressure on Russia to agree a full ceasefire.
levels.why: Cutting Russia's oil income is one of the main ways allies try to weaken its ability to fund the war in Ukraine.

levels.headline: UK sanctions every major Russian oil producer as leaders meet in Dublin
levels.body:
The UK says it is the first country to sanction all ten of Russia's major oil producers. The measures also target shadow fleet ships that carry Russian oil and liquefied natural gas, large coal companies and Rosneft's Arctic project, Vostok Oil.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the step at the ninth European Political Community summit in Dublin, hosted by Ireland. He wants leaders from about 50 countries to keep up pressure on Vladimir Putin and to back strong, legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine. He will also co-chair a Friends of Ukraine event with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin.
The government says Ukraine peace talks have made progress, but it warns against complacency and wants Russia to accept a full ceasefire.
levels.why: Sanctions on oil aim to reduce the money Russia has to pay for its war.

levels.headline: UK targets Russia's oil industry with sweeping new sanctions
levels.body:
The UK has imposed sanctions on all ten of Russia's major oil producers, the first country to do so, the government says. Tankers in the so-called shadow fleet that move Russian oil and gas, big coal companies and a major Arctic oil and gas project called Vostok Oil are also covered.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham made the announcement before the European Political Community summit in Dublin, which brings together leaders from around 50 countries. He will urge them to keep up pressure on President Putin and to offer Ukraine firm security guarantees that are legally binding. He will co-chair an event for Ukraine's supporters with Ireland's Prime Minister, Micheál Martin.
The government says peace talks have moved forward, but it is not time to relax.
levels.why: Oil sales fund much of Russia's budget, so sanctions are a key way to put pressure on it.

levels.headline: UK sanctions all of Russia's top oil producers
levels.body:
The UK government says it has put sanctions on all ten of Russia's biggest oil producers. It says it is the first country to do this. Sanctions are penalties that make it harder for companies to trade or use banks. The list also includes ships that secretly carry Russian oil, big coal firms and an Arctic oil and gas project.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced it ahead of a summit in Dublin. Leaders from around 50 European countries are meeting there. He wants them to keep up the pressure on Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, and to give Ukraine strong promises of protection.
The government says peace talks have made progress, but it does not want countries to relax.
levels.why: Cutting Russia's oil money is meant to make it harder to keep fighting in Ukraine.

levels.headline: The UK puts new penalties on Russia's biggest oil companies
levels.body:
The UK has put new penalties, called sanctions, on all ten of Russia's biggest oil companies. The government says no other country has done this. The penalties make it harder for these firms to sell oil and use banks. They also cover ships that secretly carry Russian oil and gas, and some coal firms.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, announced this before a big meeting in Dublin. Leaders from about 50 countries in Europe are there. He wants them to keep pushing Russia's president, Vladimir Putin, to end the war. He also wants Ukraine to get firm promises of protection.
The government says talks about peace are moving, but more pressure is still needed.
levels.why: Russia earns a lot from oil, so these penalties aim to make the war in Ukraine harder to pay for.

levels.headline: The UK puts a stop sign on Russia's oil companies
levels.body:
The UK has put a stop sign in front of Russia's ten biggest oil companies. The proper name for this is sanctions. It means that these companies find it much harder to sell their oil or to use banks. The UK says it is the first country to do this to all ten.
Why does it matter? Russia is fighting a war in Ukraine, and it earns a lot of money from selling oil. Some of that money pays for the war. If it earns less, it has less to spend.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, shared the news before a big meeting in Dublin. Leaders from about 50 countries are going. He wants them to keep up the pressure on Russia.
levels.why: It tries to cut the money Russia has to pay for its war.

levels.headline: The UK punishes Russia's oil firms
levels.body:
The UK has punished Russia's ten biggest oil companies. The punishment is called sanctions. It means these firms find it much harder to sell oil and use banks. The UK says it is the first country to do this to all ten.
Russia makes a lot of money selling oil. That money helps pay for its war in Ukraine. The UK wants to cut that money.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, told the news before a big meeting in Dublin. About 50 countries are going. He wants them to keep pushing Russia to stop the war. He also wants Ukraine to be told, clearly, that it will be kept safe in future.
levels.why: It tries to cut the money Russia has to pay for its war.

levels.headline: The UK says no to Russia's oil firms
levels.body:
The UK has said it will not do business with Russia's ten biggest oil companies. This is called putting sanctions on them. The UK says it is the first country to do this to all ten.
Russia sells oil to make money. That money helps it fight a war in Ukraine. If the oil firms cannot sell as easily, Russia has less money for the war.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, shared the news before a big meeting in Dublin, in Ireland. Leaders from about 50 countries are there. He wants them all to keep telling Russia to stop. He also wants Ukraine to get a firm promise that it will be kept safe.
levels.why: It aims to give Russia less money for the war in Ukraine.

levels.headline: The UK tells Russia's oil firms they cannot trade as before
levels.body:
Two countries are fighting a war. Russia started it by going into Ukraine. Russia makes money by selling oil, and some of that money pays for the war. The UK wants to cut that money.
So the UK has told Russia's ten biggest oil companies that it will not do business with them. This is called a sanction. It is a bit like a group of friends saying they will not play with someone who keeps breaking the rules.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, shared the news before a big meeting in Dublin. Leaders from about 50 countries are there to talk about helping Ukraine.
levels.why: It tries to cut Russia's money, so it is harder to keep fighting.

levels.headline: Friends agree not to play with someone who breaks the rules
levels.body:
Imagine someone in the playground keeps hurting another child. Other children might say, 'We will not share our toys with you until you stop.' That is a bit like a sanction.
Russia is fighting a war in Ukraine. It makes money from selling oil, and some of that money pays for the war. The UK has said it will not do business with Russia's ten biggest oil companies. It is the first country to do that for all ten.
The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, told everyone at a big meeting in Dublin. Leaders from about 50 countries were there. He asked them to help Ukraine and keep telling Russia to stop.
levels.why: It is a way to ask Russia to stop the war without fighting.

headline: Five EU states want UK to pay into regional funds for electricity market access

terms.meaning: EU money used to help poorer regions catch up with richer ones.
Being allowed to trade electricity across borders under shared EU rules.
An early version of an agreement that can still be changed.

levels.headline: Five EU states want UK to pay into regional funds for electricity market access
levels.body:
Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands have written to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Council President António Costa, urging that Britain's integration into the EU electricity market be made conditional on a contribution to EU regional development funds.
A draft joint EU-UK statement reportedly suggests EU leaders broadly support the principle of such a British contribution, though the text could still change before the summit on 20 November. UK Under Secretary of State Martin McCluskey has said no amount or contribution has been agreed, and that any payment would have to deliver value for money for Britain.
The Commission's draft negotiating mandate proposes a permanent, legally binding mechanism to reduce economic and social gaps between regions, with the level reflecting the size of the UK economy and its share of the internal market.
levels.why: The talks could decide how much the UK pays for closer energy ties with the EU and how far the relationship is rebuilt after Brexit.

levels.headline: Five EU countries say the UK must pay for electricity market access
levels.body:
Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands have asked EU leaders to make British access to the EU electricity market depend on a payment into EU regional development funds. They set out their position in a letter to Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa.
A draft joint statement reportedly suggests EU leaders broadly back the principle, though the wording may change before the EU-UK summit on 20 November. UK minister Martin McCluskey says no amount has been agreed and that any payment must offer value for money.
The European Commission's draft mandate describes a permanent, legally binding mechanism to narrow regional gaps, scaled to the size of the UK economy and how much of the single market it joins.
levels.why: The outcome will show how much closer UK-EU energy cooperation costs and who sets the terms.

levels.headline: EU countries demand UK contribution in return for electricity market access
levels.body:
Five EU members, Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, want Britain to pay into the EU's regional development funds if it is to be part of the EU electricity market. They made the demand in a letter to the heads of the European Commission and the European Council.
A draft joint statement reportedly shows EU leaders are broadly supportive of the idea, but it could change before a UK-EU summit on 20 November. A UK minister, Martin McCluskey, said no sum has been agreed and any payment would have to be good value for Britain.
The Commission's draft plan would create a permanent, legally binding scheme to reduce regional inequality, with the UK payment reflecting its economic size.
levels.why: Energy costs and Brexit politics meet here, and a deal could shape bills and trade for years.

levels.headline: Five EU countries want UK to pay for access to electricity market
levels.body:
Five EU countries want the UK to make a payment to the EU if it is to join the EU electricity market. They are Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. The money would go into funds that help poorer regions of the EU.
A draft statement for a UK-EU summit on 20 November reportedly suggests EU leaders mostly support the idea, though the wording could still be changed. A UK minister, Martin McCluskey, said no amount has been agreed. He said any payment must give Britain good value for money.
The EU Commission wants a lasting, legally binding system, with the UK share based on the size of its economy.
levels.why: It could affect how much the UK pays to be closer to the EU, and the price of energy.

levels.headline: Five EU countries ask the UK to pay for electricity links
levels.body:
Five countries in the EU want the UK to pay into an EU fund if it wants to trade electricity with Europe under shared rules. The countries are Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands. The fund helps poorer parts of Europe catch up.
A draft paper for a meeting between the UK and EU on 20 November reportedly says EU leaders mostly agree with the idea. A draft can still be changed. A UK minister, Martin McCluskey, said nothing has been agreed. He said any payment would have to be good value.
The EU Commission wants a long-lasting, legally binding scheme, and the UK payment would depend on the size of its economy.
levels.why: It shows that closer ties with the EU may come with a bill.

levels.headline: Five EU countries want the UK to pay to share electricity
levels.body:
Britain left the European Union in 2020. Now it wants to share electricity with EU countries again. Sharing means power can flow both ways, which can help keep lights on when the wind is low.
Five EU countries say the UK should pay money into an EU fund before that happens. The fund helps poorer areas of Europe. The countries are Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
The UK and the EU will meet on 20 November. A first draft of their agreement reportedly says EU leaders mostly like the idea. A UK minister said no amount has been agreed. He said any payment must be good value.
levels.why: It shows how much it may cost to work closely with the EU again.

levels.headline: Five EU countries want the UK to pay to share power
levels.body:
The UK left the European Union a few years ago. Now it wants to share electricity with EU countries again. Sharing power means each side can send electricity to the other when it is short.
Five EU countries say the UK should pay some money first. The money would go into a fund that helps poorer places in Europe. The five countries are Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
The UK and EU will meet on 20 November. A first draft paper says EU leaders mostly like the idea. A UK minister said nothing has been agreed yet. He said any payment must be good value for the UK.
levels.why: It shows that closer links with the EU might cost money.

levels.headline: Five countries say Britain should pay to share electricity
levels.body:
Britain used to be in a big group of European countries called the EU. It left. Now it wants to share electricity with them again. Sharing power helps if one country runs short.
Five of the EU countries say, 'If you want to share, you should pay into our fund.' The fund helps poorer places in Europe. Britain says no amount has been agreed yet. A UK minister says any payment must be good value.
The two sides will meet on 20 November to talk. A first rough paper says most EU leaders like the idea, but it could change before the meeting.
levels.why: It shows that getting closer to Europe again might come with a cost.

levels.headline: Neighbours argue about who pays to share the power
levels.body:
Imagine you live on a street with lots of neighbours. You used to share a big bag of batteries with them. Then you moved apart. Now you would like to share again, because it helps everyone when someone runs low.
Five neighbours say, 'You can share again, but you need to put some money in the jar first.' The jar is used to help the families on the street who have less. You say, 'We have not agreed any amount, and it has to be fair.'
The neighbours will meet on 20 November to talk about it.
levels.why: It shows how countries decide who pays when they share something useful.

levels.headline: Friends talk about sharing batteries
levels.body:
Imagine two groups of friends who share batteries for their toys. One group moved away. Now they would like to share again, because it helps everyone when a toy runs out of power.
Five friends in the other group say, 'You may share again, but please put a coin in our money jar first.' The jar helps friends who have less. The first group says, 'We have not agreed how many coins, and it must be fair.'
They will meet on 20 November to talk about it properly. Nobody has decided yet.
levels.why: It shows that sharing sometimes means working out who pays.

headline: UK inflation stands at 3.5% and unemployment at 4.7% before key data next week

terms.meaning: Consumer Prices Index, the main measure of UK inflation.
The share of working-age people who have a job.
Job openings that employers are trying to fill.

levels.headline: UK inflation stands at 3.5% and unemployment at 4.7% before key data next week
levels.body:
The latest official figures show UK consumer price inflation (CPI) at 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August, with the broader CPIH measure at 3.6%. Both were published on 21 October.
The Office for National Statistics also reported that unemployment was 4.7% in June to August 2026, down 0.1 percentage points on the year and on the quarter. The employment rate rose to 75.3%. The ONS described the labour market as broadly flat this year, with the number of vacancies showing its largest fall since the start of 2026.
Two important releases are due next week. Labour market figures come on 17 November, and October inflation follows at 7am on 18 November. They will feed into the Bank of England's decision on 17 December, after it raised Bank Rate to 4% and warned inflation could approach 5% by mid-2027.
levels.why: These figures guide interest rates, wages and prices, so they shape household budgets across the country.

levels.headline: UK inflation was 3.5% in September, with unemployment at 4.7%
levels.body:
The ONS reports that CPI inflation was 3.5% in September, compared with 3.1% in August. The broader CPIH measure, which includes housing costs, was 3.6%. These figures came out on 21 October.
Unemployment was 4.7% in the three months to August, a fall of 0.1 percentage points on both the quarter and the year, and the employment rate rose to 75.3%. The ONS said the labour market has been broadly flat this year, though vacancies recorded their largest fall since January.
New labour market data is published on 17 November and October inflation on 18 November. Both will be watched by the Bank of England, which has raised Bank Rate to 4% and expects inflation to approach 5% by the middle of 2027.
levels.why: Prices, jobs and interest rates are linked, so these numbers affect mortgages, wages and the cost of living.

levels.headline: UK inflation hits 3.5% while unemployment edges down to 4.7%
levels.body:
Official figures show UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, up from 3.1% in August. The broader CPIH measure, which includes housing costs, was 3.6%.
Meanwhile, unemployment was 4.7% in the June to August period, slightly lower than a year earlier. More people were in work, with the employment rate at 75.3%. The Office for National Statistics said the job market has been broadly flat this year, and the number of job vacancies has seen its biggest drop since January.
Next week brings fresh data. Labour market figures arrive on 17 November, followed by October inflation on 18 November. The Bank of England, which recently raised its main interest rate to 4%, will study both before its December meeting.
levels.why: Higher prices squeeze budgets, and the jobs picture helps decide whether interest rates rise further.

levels.headline: UK prices rose 3.5% in the year to September; unemployment is 4.7%
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, according to the Office for National Statistics. In August the figure was 3.1%. This measure is called CPI inflation. A wider measure that includes housing costs was 3.6%.
The ONS also said 4.7% of people looking for work could not find it between June and August. That is slightly lower than a year ago. About 75.3% of working-age people had a job. The job market has been fairly flat this year, and fewer vacancies are being advertised.
New figures are due next week. Jobs data comes on 17 November and October inflation on 18 November. The Bank of England will use them to decide on interest rates in December.
levels.why: The numbers affect shop prices, pay and the interest rates on loans and mortgages.

levels.headline: Prices are up 3.5% in a year, and 4.7% of workers are unemployed
levels.body:
Official figures show that prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year before. This is called inflation. In August it was 3.1%, so prices are rising faster now.
The same experts also looked at jobs. Between June and August, 4.7% of people who wanted a job could not get one. That is a little lower than a year earlier. About three in four working-age people had a job. There are fewer jobs being advertised than before.
New figures come out next week. Jobs numbers are due on 17 November and the latest price numbers on 18 November. The Bank of England will look at them before it decides what to do about interest rates in December.
levels.why: Rising prices and the job market affect how far wages and pocket money go.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster, and jobs are not growing
levels.body:
Prices in the UK went up by 3.5% over the last year. This is called inflation. It means things in the shops cost more than before. A month earlier, the figure was 3.1%, so prices are rising a little faster.
About 4.7 in every 100 people who wanted a job could not find one. That is a bit lower than last year. Most working-age people, about 75 in every 100, had a job. But fewer new jobs are being advertised.
New figures come out next week, on 17 and 18 November. The Bank of England looks at these before it decides about interest rates. It has already put them up to 4%.
levels.why: When prices rise faster than pay, families can buy less than before.

levels.headline: Prices are 3.5% higher than a year ago, and most adults who want work have it
levels.body:
Prices in the UK are 3.5% higher than they were a year ago. This is called inflation. It means a pound buys a bit less than it did. A month earlier the figure was 3.1%, so prices are rising a little faster now.
The experts also counted people without jobs. About 4.7 in every 100 people who wanted work could not find it. That is slightly better than last year. Roughly three in four working-age adults had a job. Fewer jobs are being advertised, though.
New numbers come out on 17 and 18 November. The Bank of England will look at them before it decides about interest rates. It has already raised the rate to 4% to slow price rises.
levels.why: Rising prices and the job market affect how far wages and pocket money go.

levels.headline: Things cost more than a year ago
levels.body:
Things in shops cost 3.5% more than they did a year ago. This is called inflation. For example, something that cost 100 pence last year now costs about 103 or 104 pence. A month earlier, the rise was smaller, so prices are climbing faster now.
Some people cannot find work. About 5 in every 100 people looking for a job could not get one. That is a little better than last year. But not many new jobs are being advertised.
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. It will see new numbers next week. It has already made borrowing cost more, to stop prices climbing too fast.
levels.why: It shows how far money goes in the shops and how easy it is to find work.

levels.headline: Shop prices are going up a bit faster
levels.body:
Things in the shops cost more than they did a year ago. If a snack cost 100 pence last year, it costs about 3 or 4 pence more now. This is called inflation. It was less a month ago, so it is going up faster.
Some grown-ups cannot find work. For every 100 people who want a job, about 5 do not have one. That is a little better than last year.
The Bank of England looks after the country's money. It will see new numbers next week. It has already made borrowing cost more, to stop prices going up so quickly.
levels.why: It shows how far a pound goes and whether grown-ups can find work.

levels.headline: Sweets cost a little more than last year
levels.body:
Imagine the sweets in the shop cost a little more than they did last year. If a bag cost 100 pence, it might now cost about 103 pence. When lots of things cost a bit more, that is called inflation. It was smaller last month, so prices are climbing a bit faster.
Some grown-ups are looking for work. For every 100 who want a job, about 5 cannot find one yet. That is a little better than last year.
The grown-ups at the Bank of England watch these numbers closely. More numbers come out next week. They help the Bank decide how to keep prices steady.
levels.why: It shows how far pocket money and wages go, and how easy it is for grown-ups to find work.

headline: Votes at 16 bill reaches Lords committee stage

terms.meaning: The part of a bill's journey where members examine it line by line.
The list of people who are registered to vote.
A proposed law that Parliament is considering.

levels.headline: Votes at 16 bill reaches Lords committee stage
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill has entered Lords Committee Stage in Parliament, according to a government blog post dated 2 November. The Bill would extend the voting age to 16 for all UK elections.
It would also lower the age at which people can register to vote to 14, so that young people are fully registered before an election close to their 16th birthday. Under-16s would not appear on any version of the electoral register that is made publicly available. The Bill also contains tougher rules on political finance and on foreign interference in elections.
In Committee Stage, peers examine the detail of a bill line by line. Lords Second Reading was on 14 September. The government says it wants the changes in place for the next UK general election.
levels.why: If passed, it would give around two more school-year groups a vote in every UK election.

levels.headline: Bill to lower the UK voting age to 16 is now being examined by peers
levels.body:
The Representation of the People Bill, which would lower the voting age to 16 for all UK elections, is now at Committee Stage in the House of Lords, the government said on 2 November.
The Bill would also let people register to vote from the age of 14, so they are ready before their 16th birthday. Under-16s would be kept off the publicly available versions of the electoral register. It contains further measures on political finance and on protecting elections from foreign interference.
At Committee Stage peers go through a bill line by line. The Lords gave it a Second Reading on 14 September. The government wants the new rules in force before the next general election.
levels.why: It could change who can take part in elections across the whole country.

levels.headline: Votes at 16 plan moves to the House of Lords for detailed scrutiny
levels.body:
A bill that would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in all UK elections is now being examined in detail by the House of Lords. The Representation of the People Bill reached Committee Stage, the government said on 2 November.
People would be able to register to vote at 14, so they are on the list in time for their 16th birthday, but under-16s would not appear on public versions of the register. The Bill also tightens rules on political donations and on foreign interference.
In Committee Stage, peers study each line of the bill and suggest changes. The government hopes the rules will be in place for the next general election.
levels.why: Lowering the voting age would change who decides elections and what parties talk about.

levels.headline: Plan to let 16-year-olds vote across the UK reaches the Lords
levels.body:
A bill to let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in all UK elections is now in the House of Lords. It is called the Representation of the People Bill. The government said on 2 November that peers have started the next step, called Committee Stage.
Under the plan, young people could register to vote from the age of 14, so they are ready in time. Their details would not appear on the public version of the list of voters. The bill also has new rules on political money and on stopping other countries interfering in elections.
At this stage, members of the Lords look at each part of the bill and suggest changes.
levels.why: It would let more young people have a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: A law to let 16-year-olds vote is being checked in the House of Lords
levels.body:
A proposed law would let 16 and 17-year-olds vote in every election in the UK. It is called the Representation of the People Bill. This month the House of Lords began checking it closely. This stage is called Committee Stage.
Under the plan, children could put their names on the list of voters from the age of 14. That way they are ready when they turn 16. The public would not be able to see the names of anyone under 16 on the list. The bill also adds rules about political money and about stopping other countries from interfering in elections.
The Lords go through each part and can suggest changes.
levels.why: It could mean you get a vote at 16 instead of 18.

levels.headline: Plans to let 16-year-olds vote are being checked by the House of Lords
levels.body:
The government wants 16 and 17-year-olds to be allowed to vote in all elections in the UK. At the moment you have to wait until you are 18. To change this, Parliament has to pass a new law. The proposed law is called the Representation of the People Bill.
This month the House of Lords started to check the bill closely. Members read it line by line and can suggest changes. Under the plan, young people could add their names to the list of voters at 14. The public would not see the names of people under 16.
The government wants the change to be ready for the next general election.
levels.why: If it becomes law, 16 and 17-year-olds will get a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: Could 16-year-olds soon be allowed to vote?
levels.body:
The government wants people to be able to vote at 16. At the moment you have to be 18. To change this, a new law is needed. Parliament is the group of people who decide the laws. A suggested law is called a bill.
The bill is now in the House of Lords. The people there are reading it very carefully, line by line, and can suggest changes. The plan lets young people sign up to vote at 14, so they are ready by 16. Their names would be kept private until then.
The government wants the change to be ready for the next big election.
levels.why: If it happens, young people will have a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: A new law could let 16-year-olds vote
levels.body:
Right now, you must be 18 to vote in elections. The government wants to change that to 16. To do this, it needs a new law. A new law starts as an idea called a bill. Parliament has to agree to it.
The bill is now with a group called the House of Lords. They are reading the bill carefully and may suggest changes. The plan says young people could sign up to vote at 14, so they are ready on their 16th birthday. Their names would not be shown to the public.
The government wants it to be ready for the next big election.
levels.why: It could give young people a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: People might be able to vote when they are 16
levels.body:
Right now, you have to be a grown-up to choose who runs the country. This is called voting. The government wants to let people vote from 16 instead.
To change this, they need a new rule, called a law. A group of people called the Lords is reading the idea very carefully. They can say, 'Yes,' or, 'Please change this bit.'
The plan also says young people could sign up at 14, so they are ready on their 16th birthday. Their names would be kept private.
The government hopes this will be ready before the next big vote.
levels.why: It could give young people a say in who runs the country.

levels.headline: Maybe big kids could pick the class captain
levels.body:
Imagine that only the oldest children in school were allowed to pick the class captain. Now someone says, 'Let the slightly younger big kids pick too.' That is a bit like what is being thought about for the whole country.
In the country, grown-ups choose the leaders by voting. The government wants to let people vote from 16 instead of 18. A group of wise people is reading the idea very carefully before anyone decides.
If they say yes, young people could sign up a bit earlier. The government hopes it will be ready for the next big vote.
levels.why: It might give older children a say in the people who make rules for the country.

headline: Oil rises after Trump says US does not need an Iran deal

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for crude oil.
A narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which much of the world's oil passes.
West Texas Intermediate, the main US benchmark price for oil.

levels.headline: Oil rises after Trump says US does not need an Iran deal
levels.body:
Oil prices rose on Thursday 12 November after President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that the US no longer needed a deal with Iran, writing that the US had "got their Strait", a reference to the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude settled 3.3% higher at $95.82 a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate rose 2.6% to $88.74.
The rise follows a steep fall this month. Brent is still down about 20% in November and WTI is down 16%. Brent fell below $90 on 10 November, the first time since August, after settling at $104.77 on 2 November following a 7.6% drop, on hopes of diplomacy.
Analysts warned that markets may have priced in an end to the fighting too quickly. The war with Iran is in its ninth month with no clear end in sight.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and shipping costs, and into the inflation that central banks are trying to control.

levels.headline: Oil jumps as Trump says no Iran deal is needed
levels.body:
Oil prices rose on 12 November after President Trump wrote on Truth Social that the US did not need a deal with Iran and had "got their Strait", meaning the Strait of Hormuz. Brent settled 3.3% higher at $95.82 a barrel and WTI gained 2.6% to $88.74.
Despite the rise, Brent is down about 20% this month and WTI is down 16%. Brent dipped below $90 on 10 November for the first time since August, having settled at $104.77 on 2 November after a 7.6% fall driven by hopes for diplomacy.
Some analysts said the market had priced in peace too quickly. The conflict is now in its ninth month and neither side seems to have shifted its position.
levels.why: Energy prices affect household bills and the interest rate decisions of central banks.

levels.headline: Oil prices rise after Trump rules out needing an Iran deal
levels.body:
Oil prices climbed on Thursday after President Trump said on social media that the US did not need a deal with Iran because it had "got their Strait", meaning the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude closed 3.3% higher at $95.82 a barrel. US benchmark WTI rose 2.6% to $88.74.
That still leaves prices well down on the start of the month. Brent is about 20% lower in November after peaking above $100 on hopes of talks. It had slipped under $90 on Tuesday, its lowest since August.
Analysts warned that traders may have assumed the war was ending too soon. The conflict is in its ninth month, and neither side appears to have changed its stance.
levels.why: The price of oil sets the cost of fuel and heating and can push up prices across the economy.

levels.headline: Oil prices go up after Trump says the US does not need an Iran deal
levels.body:
The price of oil went up on Thursday after US President Donald Trump said the US did not need a deal with Iran. He wrote that the US had "got their Strait". This is the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow stretch of sea that much of the world's oil travels through. Brent, the main international oil price, rose 3.3% to $95.82 a barrel.
Oil is still much cheaper than at the start of the month. Brent is down about 20% in November, because people hoped a peace deal was near. It fell below $90 earlier this week.
Experts say traders may have expected the war to end too soon. The war is in its ninth month.
levels.why: Oil prices affect what we pay for petrol and heating, and how fast prices rise.

levels.headline: Oil gets dearer after Trump says no Iran deal needed
levels.body:
The price of oil went up on Thursday. US President Donald Trump said the US did not need a deal with Iran, and that the US had control of the Strait of Hormuz. That is a narrow sea route where lots of the world's oil passes. The main world price, called Brent, rose 3.3% to $95.82 for a barrel of oil.
That is still lower than at the start of the month. People had hoped a peace deal was close, so the price fell by about a fifth. This week it dipped under $90, the lowest since August.
Some experts think traders hoped for peace too early. The war has gone on for nine months.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for petrol and heating, and they affect prices in the shops.

levels.headline: Oil costs more after Trump says there may be no deal with Iran
levels.body:
The price of oil went up on Thursday. Oil is the thick liquid that is turned into petrol and diesel. The United States and Iran are in a war. The US president, Donald Trump, said the US did not need a deal with Iran. He said the US had control of the Strait of Hormuz. That is a narrow sea route that lots of the world's oil ships travel through.
The price of a barrel of oil rose by about 3% to $95.82. Earlier this month it had been over $100 and then dropped, because people hoped for peace.
The war has lasted nine months.
levels.why: Oil prices change the cost of petrol and heating, and so how much things cost in shops.

levels.headline: Oil goes up in price after Trump comments on Iran
levels.body:
The price of oil went up on Thursday. Oil is turned into petrol and diesel. The United States and Iran have been in a war for nine months. The US president, Donald Trump, said the US did not need a deal with Iran. He said the US had control of the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow sea route that lots of the world's oil ships use.
Brent, the main world price, rose 3.3% to $95.82 a barrel. This month the price had fallen by about a fifth, because people hoped for peace. Some experts think traders believed the war was ending too soon.
When oil costs more, petrol, heating and shipping can cost more too.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for fuel and heating and can push prices up in shops.

levels.headline: Oil gets a bit dearer after Trump's words
levels.body:
The price of oil went up on Thursday. Oil is turned into petrol and diesel for cars and lorries. The United States and Iran are in a war that has gone on for nine months. The US president, Donald Trump, said the US did not need a deal with Iran to stop it.
Much of the world's oil is carried by ships through a narrow sea route called the Strait of Hormuz. If ships cannot use it easily, oil gets scarce and costs more.
Earlier this month, people hoped for peace, and the price fell a lot. Now it has gone up a little again.
levels.why: Oil prices change what we pay for petrol and heating, and the price of lots of other things.

levels.headline: Oil gets pricier because of a fight between countries
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. It is turned into petrol for cars and fuel for lorries and ships. Two countries, America and Iran, are in a war. A leader said America does not need an agreement to stop it.
Much of the world's oil is carried on ships through a narrow sea path. If the path is not safe, there is less oil to sell, so it costs more. This week, the price of oil went up a little.
Earlier this month, people hoped the war would stop, and the price went down a lot. Now people are less sure.
levels.why: Oil prices change what grown-ups pay for fuel, and the price of many other things.

levels.headline: Why a faraway quarrel can change what petrol costs
levels.body:
Imagine one narrow gate that lots of delivery lorries must drive through. If two groups of grown-ups quarrel near the gate, the lorries may not get through, and the shop may run short. When the shop runs short, it charges more.
That is a bit like what is happening with oil. Oil is what makes petrol and fuel for cars and ships. Much of it goes by ship through a narrow sea path. America and Iran are in a war near it.
A leader said this week that no deal is needed. So the price of oil went up a little.
levels.why: Oil prices change what grown-ups pay for fuel and affect the price of many things.

headline: Abu Dhabi talks on Ukraine end with prisoner exchange but no ceasefire

terms.meaning: An agreement to stop fighting, at least for a time.
A region of eastern Ukraine, part of which Russia controls.
Promises from other countries to help protect a country from future attack.

levels.headline: Abu Dhabi talks on Ukraine end with prisoner exchange but no ceasefire
levels.body:
Two days of US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi produced a large-scale prisoner exchange as their only tangible result, with no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory, according to Euronews.
Moscow rejected calls for an immediate ceasefire, insisting on wider security arrangements first, and still demands control of the whole Donbas, including areas it has not captured. Kyiv refuses to give up territory. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the talks "constructive and quite substantive", and Marco Rubio called them "very productive". US envoy Jared Kushner was more guarded, saying "we are pushing a boulder uphill" towards a Putin-Zelenskyy meeting.
On Thursday US envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Moscow for talks with Vladimir Putin, while Zelenskyy was due to meet US envoys in Dublin.
levels.why: Whether talks lead to a ceasefire decides how long the fighting, and its effect on European security and energy prices, continues.

levels.headline: Ukraine-Russia talks in Abu Dhabi end without ceasefire
levels.body:
The US-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi ended after two days with an agreement on a large prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on a ceasefire or on territory.
Russia has rejected an immediate ceasefire and wants broader security arrangements first. It still demands the whole of the Donbas region, including parts it has failed to capture, while Ukraine will not give up land. President Zelenskyy described the talks as "constructive and quite substantive". Marco Rubio said they were "very productive", but envoy Jared Kushner said "we are pushing a boulder uphill".
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner then travelled to Moscow to see President Putin. Zelenskyy was expected to meet US envoys in Dublin.
levels.why: Peace in Ukraine would affect Europe's security, its energy costs and the cost of supporting Kyiv.

levels.headline: Abu Dhabi peace talks deliver a prisoner swap but no ceasefire
levels.body:
Talks between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi, mediated by the United States, finished after two days with a large prisoner exchange but no agreement on a ceasefire or on land.
Moscow turned down an immediate halt to fighting and wants wider security arrangements first. It also wants the whole Donbas region of eastern Ukraine, which Kyiv refuses to hand over. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, called the talks constructive, and Marco Rubio, called them very productive. US envoy Jared Kushner said the effort felt like pushing a boulder uphill.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Kushner went to Moscow on Thursday to meet Vladimir Putin.
levels.why: The talks show how far apart the two sides still are on ending the war.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia hold talks in Abu Dhabi but no ceasefire agreed
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia held two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, with the United States acting as go-between. They agreed a large exchange of prisoners, but they did not agree a ceasefire or what should happen to Ukrainian land.
Russia says it will not stop fighting straight away and wants wider security deals first. It also wants all of the Donbas region in eastern Ukraine, but Ukraine will not give up territory. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, called the talks useful. A US envoy, Jared Kushner, said it was like pushing a boulder uphill.
On Thursday, US envoys travelled to Moscow to meet President Putin.
levels.why: A ceasefire would stop the fighting, so the lack of one matters for Ukraine and the rest of Europe.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia talk in Abu Dhabi but still no ceasefire
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia met for two days of talks in Abu Dhabi. The United States helped by acting as a go-between. The two sides agreed to swap a large number of prisoners. But they did not agree to stop the fighting, which is called a ceasefire.
Russia wants more promises about security before it stops. It also wants a whole region of eastern Ukraine, called the Donbas. Ukraine says no to giving up land. Ukraine's president called the talks useful. An American helper, Jared Kushner, said it felt like pushing a very heavy rock uphill.
On Thursday, American envoys went to Moscow to speak with Russia's president, Vladimir Putin.
levels.why: Without a ceasefire, people in Ukraine remain in danger and Europe stays worried about its safety.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia talk, but the fighting goes on
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia met for two days in Abu Dhabi to talk about ending their war. The United States helped them to talk. They agreed to swap many prisoners. But they did not agree to stop fighting.
Russia wants more promises about safety before it stops. It also wants a big part of eastern Ukraine called the Donbas. Ukraine says it will not give away land. An American helper said trying to get peace was like pushing a heavy rock uphill.
Now American helpers are going to Moscow, where they will talk to Russia's leader, Vladimir Putin.
levels.why: Until the fighting stops, people in Ukraine are not safe, and the war affects the rest of Europe too.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia talk in Abu Dhabi, but no ceasefire yet
levels.body:
Ukraine and Russia met for two days of talks in Abu Dhabi, and the United States helped them to talk. They agreed to swap a large number of prisoners. But they did not agree on a ceasefire, which means a stop to the fighting.
Russia wants more security promises first, and it wants all of a region called the Donbas. Ukraine says it will not give up land. Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said the talks were useful. An American envoy, Jared Kushner, said it felt like pushing a boulder uphill.
On Thursday, American envoys went to Moscow to speak to Russia's president, Vladimir Putin.
levels.why: Without a ceasefire, people in Ukraine stay in danger and Europe stays worried about its security.

levels.headline: Ukraine and Russia talk, but there is still no peace
levels.body:
Russia and Ukraine are at war. For two days, they sat down and talked in a place called Abu Dhabi. America helped them. The two sides agreed to swap many prisoners, so some families can see their loved ones again.
But they did not agree to stop fighting. Russia wants a big part of Ukraine called the Donbas. Ukraine says no. One American helper said making peace was like pushing a heavy rock up a hill.
Now the helpers are going to Moscow to speak with Russia's leader. People hope the talking goes on.
levels.why: It shows how hard it is to end a war, and it matters to everyone's safety in Europe.

levels.headline: Two sides talk but cannot agree to stop
levels.body:
Two countries are in a war. Their names are Russia and Ukraine. For two days they sat in a room and talked. A friend called America helped them to talk.
They agreed to swap prisoners, so some families can be together again. That is good news. But they did not agree to stop fighting. Russia wants some of Ukraine's land. Ukraine says no, it belongs to us.
It is a bit like two children both holding the same toy. A grown-up helper said it was like pushing a heavy rock uphill. The helpers will keep trying to talk.
levels.why: It shows how hard peace can be.

levels.headline: Two sides talk but still cannot agree
levels.body:
Imagine two children arguing in the playground. Both say the same toy is theirs. A grown-up sits them down to talk it through. They talk for two whole days.
They do manage to agree on one thing. They will let each other's friends go home. That is good news. But they do not agree about the toy, so the arguing carries on.
This is a bit like Russia and Ukraine, two countries in a war. The grown-up helper, called America, says it is like pushing a heavy rock uphill. But the helpers will keep trying.
levels.why: It shows why it can take such a long time to end a war.

headline: EU budget row erupts as four countries defy Merz over Ukraine aid

terms.meaning: When every member must agree before a decision can pass.
The power to block a decision.
EU money to help poorer regions catch up with richer ones.

levels.headline: EU budget row erupts as four countries defy Merz over Ukraine aid
levels.body:
Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria have rejected German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's demand that the EU's next long-term budget depend on new funding for Ukraine, according to Euronews. In a letter to Council President António Costa, Merz called new Ukraine aid an "essential prerequisite" for approving the budget.
Both the budget and Ukraine funding need unanimity, so any one member can block them. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico called the move a "textbook case of blackmail" and threatened a veto. Brussels has promised to cover about €45 billion of Ukraine's €70 billion funding gap through a mechanism still to be defined. The four countries want to opt out of any future Ukraine loan, and Hungary's Péter Magyar said the two files are distinct.
Costa said he would set aside time for a broad discussion on Ukraine at the informal European Council in Dublin.
levels.why: The dispute could delay the EU's next budget and the money Ukraine relies on to keep running.

levels.headline: Four EU states push back against Merz's link between budget and Ukraine aid
levels.body:
Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria oppose a demand by Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz that the EU's next long-term budget be tied to new funding for Ukraine. Merz called new aid an "essential prerequisite" in a letter to Council President António Costa.
Both issues require every member state to agree. Slovakia's Prime Minister Robert Fico called the link "blackmail" and threatened a veto. Brussels has pledged to cover about €45 billion of Ukraine's €70 billion gap through a tool not yet defined. The four countries want to opt out of any future loan to Ukraine, and Hungary's Péter Magyar said the two matters should be kept separate.
Costa plans a broad discussion on Ukraine at the informal summit in Dublin.
levels.why: A failure to agree could leave both the EU budget and Ukraine's finances uncertain.

levels.headline: EU budget row: four countries reject Merz's Ukraine aid ultimatum
levels.body:
Four EU countries, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria, have refused to accept German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's demand that the next EU long-term budget be linked to fresh money for Ukraine. Merz said new aid was an "essential prerequisite".
Because both decisions need all members to agree, any country can block them. Slovakia's Robert Fico called the demand "a textbook case of blackmail" and threatened a veto. The EU has promised to cover around €45 billion of Ukraine's €70 billion funding gap, but the method is not yet decided. The four want to opt out of any future loan, and Hungary's Péter Magyar said the issues are separate.
EU Council President António Costa wants a wide talk on Ukraine in Dublin.
levels.why: The row shows how divided the EU is on paying for Ukraine.

levels.headline: Four EU countries oppose Merz over EU budget and Ukraine aid
levels.body:
