Four EU countries, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria, have said no to a demand from German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. He wants the EU's next long-term budget to depend on new money for Ukraine. In a letter, he called the new aid essential.
For both the budget and the Ukraine money, every EU country must agree. So any one country can block them. Slovakia's leader, Robert Fico, called the demand "blackmail" and threatened to veto it. The EU has promised to cover about €45 billion of the €70 billion that Ukraine needs, but it has not yet decided how. The four countries do not want to join any future loan for Ukraine.
EU leaders will talk about Ukraine in Dublin.
levels.why: The argument could delay both the EU budget and the money Ukraine needs.

levels.headline: Four EU countries say no to Germany's plan to link the budget to Ukraine aid
levels.body:
Four countries in the European Union, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria, have said no to a plan from Germany's leader, Friedrich Merz. He wants the EU's next big budget to depend on more money for Ukraine. He called new help for Ukraine essential.
All EU countries have to agree to the budget and to the money for Ukraine. That means any one country can block them. Slovakia's leader, Robert Fico, said Germany's plan was "blackmail" and said he might block it. The EU has promised to pay for about two thirds of what Ukraine is short of. It has not yet decided how.
The four countries do not want to take part in a new loan for Ukraine.
levels.why: If the EU cannot agree, its budget and help for Ukraine could be delayed.

levels.headline: Four EU countries argue with Germany over money for Ukraine
levels.body:
The European Union is a group of 27 countries. Every few years they agree a big budget, which is a plan for how to spend money. Germany's leader, Friedrich Merz, says the next budget should only go ahead if there is also new money to help Ukraine.
Four countries, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria, say no. Slovakia's leader called Germany's plan "blackmail". He said he might use a veto, which means he could stop the whole plan.
All the countries must agree before the budget or the money can move forward. Ukraine is short of money for its war. The EU has promised to cover part of it. The leaders will talk more in Dublin.
levels.why: If the countries cannot agree, both the EU's budget and help for Ukraine could be held up.

levels.headline: Four EU countries oppose Germany's plan to tie the budget to Ukraine aid
levels.body:
Four countries in the European Union say no to a plan from Germany's leader, Friedrich Merz. He wants the EU's next big budget to depend on new money for Ukraine. The four countries are Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria.
Every EU country must agree to the budget and to the money for Ukraine, so any one of them can block it. Slovakia's leader, Robert Fico, called the plan "blackmail" and said he might veto it. The EU has promised to cover about €45 billion of the €70 billion that Ukraine is missing, but has not decided how.
The four countries do not want to join any new loan for Ukraine. Leaders will talk about it in Dublin.
levels.why: If the EU cannot agree, its budget and help for Ukraine could both be delayed.

levels.headline: Four countries argue about money for Ukraine
levels.body:
The European Union is a group of 27 countries. They share a budget, which is a plan for spending money. Germany's leader wants the budget to go ahead only if there is also new money to help Ukraine. Ukraine is in a war and is short of money.
Four countries say no. They are Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria. Slovakia's leader said Germany's plan was unfair, like blackmail. He said he might use a veto. A veto means he could stop the whole plan.
All the countries have to agree before the budget can move forward. So the leaders will talk about it more in a city called Dublin.
levels.why: If the countries cannot agree, the budget and the help for Ukraine may be delayed.

levels.headline: Some countries argue about sharing money for a neighbour
levels.body:
Imagine 27 families on a street. They each put money in a shared pot for things the whole street needs. This is like the European Union's budget.
One family says, 'Let's also give more to a neighbour who is in trouble. Ukraine is in a war.' Four other families say, 'We do not want to be forced to do that.' One of them says that tying the two things together is not fair.
Every family must say yes before the pot can be used. So now they must talk it over some more. They will meet in Dublin.
levels.why: If they cannot agree, the shared pot may be held up, and so might help for Ukraine.

levels.headline: The class argues about sharing the snack money
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a snack fund that everyone puts money into. The teacher in charge wants to use some to help a classmate from another class who is in trouble. Four children say, 'No, we do not want to do that.'
The rule of the class is that everyone must say yes before the money is used. So just one child saying no can stop the whole thing.
This is a bit like what is happening in the European Union, a group of 27 countries. They are arguing about money to help a country called Ukraine. They will meet again soon to try to agree.
levels.why: Everyone must agree before the money can be used, so one 'no' can slow things down.

headline: Spain holds first general strike in 14 years over housing and wages

terms.meaning: A strike by workers across many industries at the same time.
The lowest hourly or monthly pay that employers are allowed to pay.
An election called earlier than expected.

levels.headline: Spain holds first general strike in 14 years over housing and wages
levels.body:
Spain held its first general strike in 14 years on Wednesday 11 November, called to protest the housing crisis and low wages. Authorities estimated around 120,000 people marched through central Madrid. Unions said the action was a success, while employers called it a failure.
The two largest unions, CCOO and UGT, led the call, joined by CGT, CNT and housing groups, under the slogan "wages, housing and prices". Riot police clashed with masked protesters in Madrid and Barcelona, and more than 70 people were arrested. Rents have risen by roughly 80% over the past decade while wages have lagged behind, and the unions want at least a 7% rise in the minimum wage for 2027.
The strike comes less than three weeks before a snap election on 29 November, putting housing at the centre of the campaign.
levels.why: It shows how housing costs are driving political anger across Europe and could shape Spain's election.

levels.headline: Spain's first general strike in 14 years targets housing costs and low pay
levels.body:
Spain's first general strike for 14 years took place on Wednesday 11 November, over the cost of housing and low wages. Authorities said about 120,000 people marched in central Madrid. Unions called the day a success, and employers called it a failure.
The two biggest unions, CCOO and UGT, led it with other unions and housing groups, using the slogan "wages, housing and prices". There were clashes between riot police and masked protesters in Madrid and Barcelona, with more than 70 arrests. Rents have risen by about 80% in ten years while pay has fallen behind. Unions want the minimum wage raised by at least 7% for 2027.
Spain votes in a snap election on 29 November.
levels.why: Housing costs are a major political issue, and the strike puts pressure on parties before the vote.

levels.headline: Spain grinds to a halt in first general strike for 14 years
levels.body:
Spain saw its first general strike in 14 years on Wednesday, called over the housing crisis and low pay. About 120,000 people marched through central Madrid, according to authorities. Unions said the strike worked, while employers said it failed.
The main unions, CCOO and UGT, organised the walkout with other unions and housing groups. Riot police clashed with masked protesters in Madrid and Barcelona, and more than 70 people were arrested. Rents have risen by around 80% over the past decade, and wages have not kept up. The unions are asking for a minimum wage rise of at least 7% in 2027.
The protest came less than three weeks before a snap election on 29 November.
levels.why: Many young Europeans struggle with rent, so Spain's protest is watched elsewhere too.

levels.headline: Spain holds its first general strike in 14 years over housing costs
levels.body:
Workers across Spain went on strike on Wednesday in protest at high housing costs and low pay. It was the first general strike there in 14 years. A general strike is when workers in many different industries stop work at the same time. About 120,000 people marched in Madrid, according to the authorities.
Unions said the day was a success. Employers said it was a failure. Some protesters clashed with riot police in Madrid and Barcelona, and more than 70 people were arrested.
Rents in Spain have risen by about 80% in ten years, but pay has risen much less. The unions want the minimum wage to rise by at least 7% next year. A snap election is on 29 November.
levels.why: Housing costs affect young people across Europe, and Spain's election could be shaped by this issue.

levels.headline: Workers in Spain strike over housing costs and low pay
levels.body:
Workers across Spain stopped work on Wednesday to protest about high housing costs and low pay. This kind of strike is called a general strike. It had not happened in Spain for 14 years. Around 120,000 people marched in Madrid, the authorities said.
Unions said the strike worked. Employers said it did not. Some protesters clashed with police in Madrid and Barcelona, and more than 70 people were arrested.
Rents in Spain have gone up by about 80% in ten years, but wages have not gone up as much. The unions want the lowest legal pay to go up by at least 7% next year. Spain will have an early election on 29 November.
levels.why: High rents are a worry for many young people, and this protest could affect who wins the election.

levels.headline: Many workers in Spain went on strike over rent and pay
levels.body:
On Wednesday, workers all over Spain went on strike. They said that homes cost too much and pay is too low. This sort of strike, when many different jobs stop at once, had not happened in Spain for 14 years. About 120,000 people marched in the city of Madrid.
The unions, which are groups that speak for workers, said it went well. The bosses said it did not. Some people clashed with police in Madrid and Barcelona, and more than 70 were arrested.
Rents have gone up by about 80% in ten years, but pay has not gone up as much. Spain has an early election on 29 November.
levels.why: Paying for a home is hard for many people, and this could change how people vote.

levels.headline: Workers across Spain strike over rent and low pay
levels.body:
On Wednesday, workers across Spain went on strike. They said homes cost too much and pay is too low. A strike where many different jobs stop at the same time is called a general strike, and Spain had not had one for 14 years. About 120,000 people marched through Madrid, the authorities said.
Unions, which speak for workers, said it was a success. Employers said it was not. Some protesters clashed with police in Madrid and Barcelona, and more than 70 people were arrested.
Rents have risen by about 80% in ten years, while pay has not risen as much. Spain holds an early election on 29 November.
levels.why: Rents worry many young people, and this protest could affect how people vote.

levels.headline: People in Spain protest because homes cost too much
levels.body:
On Wednesday, lots of people in Spain did not go to work. They went on strike. They said that homes cost too much, and pay is too low. It was the first time in 14 years that this many jobs stopped at once.
About 120,000 people marched through the city of Madrid. Unions, which speak for workers, said it went well. Bosses said it did not. Some people clashed with police, and more than 70 were arrested.
The cost of renting a home has gone up by about 80% in ten years. Pay has not gone up as much. Spain has an early vote for its leaders in a few weeks.
levels.why: Homes cost a lot for many families, and people use votes to say what they want to change.

levels.headline: People in Spain stopped work because homes cost too much
levels.body:
In Spain, many grown-ups stopped going to work for one day. This is called a strike. They did it to say that homes cost too much to rent, and pay is too small.
The cost of renting a home has gone up by about 80% in ten years. Pay has not gone up as much. So some families find it hard to afford a home.
About 120,000 people marched through the city of Madrid. Some people shouted and pushed with the police, and some were arrested. Spain will choose its leaders in a vote soon, and this may be a big topic.
levels.why: It shows that high rents worry many people.

levels.headline: Grown-ups in Spain said no to work for a day
levels.body:
In Spain, many grown-ups did not go to work for one day. They did this to tell the people in charge, 'Homes cost too much, and we are not paid enough.' This is called a strike.
Imagine your family had to pay more and more for your home, but the money from work stayed about the same. That would feel unfair. That is how many families in Spain feel.
About 120,000 people marched in the big city of Madrid. Soon, Spain will have a vote to choose its leaders, and this is a big topic.
levels.why: It shows how worried many families are about paying for their home.

headline: Hot US inflation data raises chances of Federal Reserve hike in December

terms.meaning: Consumer Price Index, a measure of how fast prices are rising.
The CPI measure that leaves out food and energy, which swing a lot.
The central bank of the United States.

levels.headline: Hot US inflation data raises chances of Federal Reserve hike in December
levels.body:
US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from September, above economists' forecasts, while core CPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% against an expected 0.2%. Because of last year's government shutdown, the Bureau of Labor Statistics did not publish an annual rate for October. Bank of America estimated annual inflation at 3.8% for headline and 2.7% for core.
The Federal Reserve raised its policy rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4% in September, its first rise since 2023, and held in October. After the data, markets priced an 88% chance of a quarter-point hike in December and about 11% for a half-point rise. Governor Waller said a 50 basis point rise should be considered if inflation came in high, while Cleveland's Beth Hammack does not think that is necessary for now.
The Fed meets on 8 and 9 December.
levels.why: US interest rates influence global borrowing costs, the dollar and share prices, including in the UK.

levels.headline: US inflation comes in hotter than expected, pointing to another Fed hike
levels.body:
US consumer prices increased by 0.4% in October, more than economists had forecast. Core prices, which leave out food and energy, rose 0.3% against an expected 0.2%. An annual figure was not published because of last year's government shutdown, but Bank of America estimated 3.8% for headline inflation and 2.7% for core.
The Federal Reserve lifted its rate to a range of 3.75% to 4% in September, the first increase since 2023, and left it unchanged in October. Traders now see an 88% chance of a quarter-point rise in December and 11% for a half-point rise. Governor Waller said a bigger rise should be considered, but Cleveland's Beth Hammack does not think it is needed for now.
The Fed meets on 8 and 9 December.
levels.why: Higher US rates can lift borrowing costs worldwide and shake share prices.

levels.headline: Hotter US inflation raises odds of December interest rate rise
levels.body:
Prices in the US rose by 0.4% in October, more than economists expected, official data showed. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3%, against a forecast of 0.2%. The government did not publish a yearly figure because of last year's shutdown, but Bank of America estimated headline inflation at 3.8% and core inflation at 2.7%.
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September to a range of 3.75% to 4%, its first rise since 2023, and held them in October. After the new data, traders put the chance of a quarter-point rise in December at 88%. Fed Governor Waller said a half-point rise should be considered. The Fed next meets on 8 and 9 December.
levels.why: What the Fed does affects mortgages, savings and share prices well beyond the US.

levels.headline: US prices rise faster than expected, so another interest rate rise looks likely
levels.body:
Prices in the US rose by 0.4% in October compared with September. Economists had expected less. Prices without food and energy, called core prices, rose 0.3%. A yearly figure was not published because of a government shutdown last year, but a bank estimated it at about 3.8%.
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, raised its interest rate in September to between 3.75% and 4%. It was the first rise since 2023. Now traders think there is an 88% chance of another small rise in December. One Fed official, Waller, said a bigger rise should be considered. The Fed meets on 8 and 9 December.
levels.why: US interest rates affect borrowing costs around the world, including loans and savings.

levels.headline: US prices rise faster than expected, so interest rates may go up again
levels.body:
Prices in the United States went up by 0.4% in October. That is more than experts expected. Prices for things other than food and energy rose 0.3%. A yearly figure was not published because of a government shutdown last year, but one bank thinks it is about 3.8%.
The US central bank, called the Federal Reserve, put up its interest rate in September. Now many traders think it will do it again in December, with an 88% chance of a small rise. One of its leaders, Waller, said a larger rise might be needed. The Fed meets on 8 and 9 December.
levels.why: What the US does with interest rates can change loan and savings rates around the world.

levels.headline: US prices are rising fast, so interest rates may go up
levels.body:
Prices in the United States rose by 0.4% in October. That was more than experts expected. When prices keep rising, it is called inflation. A bank thinks that over a whole year, prices are up about 3.8%.
The United States has a central bank, called the Federal Reserve. It looks after the country's money. It put up its interest rate in September. Interest is the extra you pay when you borrow. The bank does this to slow price rises.
Many traders now think it will do it again in December. They think there is an 88% chance of a small rise. The bank meets on 8 and 9 December.
levels.why: What the US does with interest rates changes borrowing costs in many countries.

levels.headline: US prices rise faster than expected, so interest rates may go up again
levels.body:
Prices in the United States rose by 0.4% in October, which was more than experts expected. When prices keep rising, it is called inflation. A bank thinks that over a whole year prices are up about 3.8%.
The United States has a central bank called the Federal Reserve. It looks after the country's money. In September it raised its interest rate, which is the extra people pay when they borrow. It did that to slow price rises.
Now many traders think it will raise the rate again in December, with an 88% chance of a small rise. The bank meets on 8 and 9 December to decide.
levels.why: What America does with interest rates can change borrowing costs in many countries.

levels.headline: US prices are going up fast, so borrowing may cost more
levels.body:
Prices in America went up by 0.4% in October. That was a bit more than experts thought. When prices keep going up, it is called inflation. Over a whole year, prices might be up about 3.8%.
America has a bank for the whole country, called the Federal Reserve. It put up its interest rate in September. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow. When borrowing costs more, people spend less, and prices slow down.
Many people now think the bank will do it again in December. It will meet on 8 and 9 December to decide.
levels.why: What America does with interest rates can change loan and savings costs elsewhere too.

levels.headline: America's prices are going up and the big bank may act
levels.body:
Prices in America went up in October. They went up more than experts thought. When prices keep going up, it is called inflation. It means your pocket money buys less than before.
America has a big bank for the whole country, called the Federal Reserve. It can make borrowing cost more. When borrowing costs more, people spend less, and prices slow down.
The bank did this once already, in September. Many people think it will do it again in December. It will meet on 8 and 9 December to decide.
levels.why: It can affect how much grown-ups pay when they borrow, in America and elsewhere.

levels.headline: The sweet shop prices are going up, so the grown-ups may step in
levels.body:
Imagine the sweet shop raises its prices again. Your pocket money buys fewer sweets. When this happens to a whole country it is called inflation. In America, prices went up more than people thought.
The grown-ups at America's big bank can help. They can make it cost a bit more to borrow money. Then people spend a bit less, and shops stop raising prices so quickly. They already did this once in September.
Many people think they will do it again in December. They meet on 8 and 9 December to decide.
levels.why: It tries to stop prices rising too fast so that pocket money and wages keep their value.
